theme: Jeremiah in the cistern; Jerusalem falls; he is freed
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 37:1-39:18. These are the chapters of the final siege. Jeremiah is arrested, thrown into a cistern, rescued by a foreigner, and finally freed when Jerusalem falls. Read it as a story of faithfulness costing everything and being vindicated.
settingTheScene: The final siege of Jerusalem lasted about eighteen months, from 588 to 586 BC. Jeremiah was accused of deserting to the enemy because he told people to surrender. He was beaten and imprisoned. The officials then dropped him into a muddy cistern to die. Chapter 39 records the city’s fall, which the prophet had announced for forty years.
observation: “You are going over to the Chaldeans!” (37:13).
“Is there any word from the LORD? … There is… You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon” (37:17).
“Then they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern… and Jeremiah sank in the mud” (38:6).
“Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch… went from the king’s house and said to the king, My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah” (38:7-9).
“Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you” (38:20).
“In the ninth year of Zedekiah… a breach was made in the city” (39:1-2).
“The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes… and put out the eyes of Zedekiah” (39:6-7).
“I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD… because you have put your trust in me” (39:17-18).
interpretation:
Zedekiah is the central tragic figure. He is afraid of the officials, afraid of the people, and afraid of the Babylonians. He wants Jeremiah’s counsel but will not follow it. He meets the prophet secretly and asks, “Is there any word from the LORD?” The answer is the same: surrender. “If you will go out… your life shall be spared.” But the fear of men is a snare. He says, “I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans.” The king who might have saved the city is paralyzed.

The cistern scene is vivid. The officials, angry that Jeremiah is weakening morale, drop him in a muddy pit to die. He sinks into the mire. It is a picture of a righteous person abandoned. Then comes an unlikely rescuer: Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian official in the palace. He risks his own position to speak to the king, and he pulls Jeremiah out with ropes padded with old rags so that they do not cut his arms. A foreigner shows more mercy than the leaders of God’s people. He is promised in return: “I will surely save you.”

Chapter 39 is the long-awaited end. The wall is breached, the temple burned, Zedekiah’s sons killed before his eyes, and then his eyes put out. The prophet’s words come true in detail. Yet the Babylonian commander treats Jeremiah kindly. He is released and stays among the poor who are left in the land.

The story shows that faithfulness to God’s word can be costly, and that vindication, though sometimes slow, is sure. And it shows how God honors acts of faith and mercy, even from an outsider.
connection: Jesus was condemned by religious leaders who feared the people (Luke 22:2), and by Pilate who feared the crowd (John 19:12-16). A foreigner, Simon of Cyrene, carried his cross (Luke 23:26). Matthew 25:40 says that what you do for the least of these you do for him. Acts 8:26-39 records an Ethiopian official’s conversion. Proverbs 29:25 says, “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.”
application:
Ask where the fear of man holds you back from obeying God.

Be an Ebed-melech this week: act on behalf of someone who is being treated unjustly, even at some cost.

Remember Jeremiah when you are faithful and it costs you. God sees.
prayerPrompts: Confess the fear of man that has trapped you.
Ask him for courage like Jeremiah’s and compassion like Ebed-melech’s.
Thank him for delivering his servants.
